analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated fund and enforcement rules to clean up radioactive and hazardous contamination at federal nuclear weapons facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 14 cosponsors and a Senate committee hearing in May 1990, but was never reported out of committee or voted on, and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced the Department of Energy and its private contractors to clean up decades of radioactive and hazardous waste at federal nuclear weapons sites like Hanford. It set up a dedicated Treasury fund for cleanup, required site-by-site cleanup plans developed with affected states and Indian tribes, made DOE and its contractors pay environmental fines out of their own budgets instead of passing them to taxpayers, and banned the contract clauses that had shielded contractors from liability. Grants would have let states and tribes independently monitor the sites.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near DOE nuclear sites — including downwind communities, tribes with treaty rights to contaminated waters, and states like Washington that host facilities — gain mandated cleanup plans, public disclosure of contamination surveys, and grants to independently monitor federal facilities. Taxpayers gain because environmental fines would come out of DOE's operating budget and contractors' fees, not a pass-through account.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near DOE nuclear weapons sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires an environmental baseline survey of every federal nuclear site, identifying contaminated land, water, aquifers, and nearby populations, and makes the results public on request [S3].

Requires compliance plans and site management plans, developed with the concurrence of affected states, tribes, and the EPA, to bring each facility into compliance with federal environmental law [S3].

Makes penalties against DOE come out of its own operating budget and penalties against contractors be paid by the contractor, and voids contract provisions that indemnify contractors against such penalties [S3].

Authorizes grants to affected states and Indian tribes to independently monitor, test, and evaluate federal nuclear facilities and to assess public health, economic, and environmental impacts, including along radioactive waste transport corridors [S3].

States a goal of restoring environments affected by releases from federal nuclear facilities within 30 years and of characterizing, stabilizing, and disposing of stored high-level and transuranic waste [S3].

analysis.who_pays: DOE contractors operating nuclear facilities would bear fines and lose liability protections; commercial and federal users of DOE nuclear services (such as uranium enrichment customers) would pay user fees covering their share of cleanup costs; and appropriations — $2.5 billion for fiscal 1991 and $3.7 billion for 1992 — would be drawn from the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes $2.5 billion for fiscal 1991 and $3.7 billion for 1992, a large new mandatory stream of federal spending on top of existing DOE budgets [S3].

It creates a new Senate-confirmed Office of Environmental Management and Remedial Action and overlapping survey, compliance, and site-management planning requirements, adding administrative structure and reporting duties to an already sprawling cleanup effort [S3].

Its 30-year restoration goal and cleanup schedules depend on technology for treating high-level and transuranic waste that was still under development, so timelines risked being unrealistic and costly to revise [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cleanup burden was real: DOE weapons sites held decades of radioactive and chemical contamination, and the bill's core idea — that the agency and its contractors should pay their own fines and publish honest surveys of contamination — addressed a genuine accountability gap. The costs were large but largely a matter of paying eventually for cleanup that could not be avoided, with the funding spread across DOE programs, other agencies, and commercial users of DOE services. The main honest objection is design, not direction: new offices and overlapping plans added bureaucratic layers, and the 30-year goal outran available waste-treatment technology. On balance the bill traded real money for enforceable cleanup schedules and public disclosure.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which held one hearing in May 1990, but the committee never reported it and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Sen. Brock Adams introduced the bill on August 1, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill, twelve Democrats and two Republicans [S4].
The committee held hearings on May 17, 1990, printed as S.Hrg. 101-716, but took no further action [S5].
No markup, floor vote, or House action followed; the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: DOE and its nuclear site contractors stayed shielded from paying their own environmental fines, and communities near sites like Hanford went without the mandated cleanup plans and independent monitoring this bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DOE contractors and the department itself

for.name: Sen. Brock Adams
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, whose provisions responded to contamination at DOE sites including Hanford in his home state

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chaired by a Democrat in the 101st Congress)
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on May 17, 1990, but never marked up or reported the bill, keeping it from the Senate floor

sides.party_line_note: Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill — 12 of the 55 Democrats and 2 of the 45 Republicans — and the record shows no party-line opposition vote, only inaction in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have made contractors pay environmental penalties out of their own pockets and voided contract clauses that indemnified them against such penalties, ending a shield under which taxpayers effectively absorbed their fines [S3]. The bill died, so that protection remained in place.

industries.industry: Environmental remediation and cleanup engineering firms
industries.note: A dedicated fund of $2.5 billion for fiscal 1991 rising to $3.7 billion for 1992, plus research and technology-transfer contracts, would have financed decades of cleanup, surveying, and waste-treatment work [S3]. The bill never became law, so this work remained subject to ordinary DOE appropriations.

industries.industry: Commercial users of DOE nuclear services (uranium enrichment customers, utilities, isotope buyers)
industries.note: The bill would have assessed user fees to recover these entities' proportionate share of cleanup costs [S3], a new expense, but one tied to services they received and contamination the cleanup addressed.

industries.industry: Department of Energy and its defense nuclear programs
industries.note: DOE would have faced mandatory fines from its own operating budget, enforceable compliance plans with state and tribal concurrence, and public contamination surveys [S3], losing the discretion it held over the weapons complex cleanup.
